questions.question: N threads need mutual exclusion on hardware that offers no test-and-set or CAS; each thread takes the next number like a deli ticket and the lowest (number, ID) pair enters first. Which algorithm is this?
questions.explanation: Lamport's bakery algorithm gives each contender a ticket number and orders entry lexicographically on (number, ID), providing mutual exclusion using only atomic reads and writes.

questions.question: A CAS-based stack guarantees that, whatever the interleaving, some thread completes a push in bounded attempts — though an individual thread may keep losing and starve. Which progress property does it satisfy?
questions.explanation: Lock-free guarantees system-wide progress: at least one operation always completes. It permits individual starvation, which is what separates it from the stronger wait-free guarantee.

questions.question: A real-time data structure must promise that every thread finishes its operation within a bounded number of its own steps — no thread may ever be starved by the others. Which progress property is required?
questions.explanation: Wait-free bounds every thread's completion in its own steps, so no starvation is possible — strictly stronger than lock-free, which only guarantees some thread progresses.

questions.question: To build a spinlock, code needs a single instruction that reads a memory word's old value and writes a new one in one indivisible bus transaction — without needing a LOCK prefix. Which x86 instruction does this?
questions.explanation: XCHG swaps a register with a memory operand atomically (it implies a bus lock), so a spinlock loop can grab the lock word and inspect the previous owner in one step.

questions.question: Low-priority task L (priority 3) holds a mutex when high-priority task H (priority 9) blocks on it, and medium tasks keep preempting L. Under the fix that lends H's priority to L, at what priority does L run until it releases the mutex?
questions.explanation: Priority inheritance elevates the holder to the highest blocked waiter's priority: L runs at 9, so medium-priority tasks can no longer preempt it and H unblocks sooner.

questions.question: A parallel sort uses 8 worker threads, and none may begin phase 2 until every worker has finished phase 1. The team installs a synchronization point initialized for 8; seven workers have arrived. How many are running?
questions.explanation: A barrier releases its waiters only when the last of the 8 threads arrives; until then every arrived thread sleeps, so all seven are blocked.

questions.question: A database lets transactions read and write freely without locks, then validates each transaction at commit and aborts it if it conflicted — cheap whenever conflicts are rare. Which concurrency-control scheme is this?
questions.explanation: OCC skips locking during execution, validates before commit, and retries losers — winning when conflicts are rare but wasting work when they are frequent.

questions.question: A global lookup table must be initialized lazily and exactly once, even though 16 threads may race to trigger the initialization simultaneously. Which synchronization construct guarantees single execution?
questions.explanation: A once flag (call_once/pthread_once) runs the initializer exactly once: the first caller executes it while racers block, and later callers skip it entirely.

questions.question: A lock-free flag/data protocol works on x86 but breaks on ARM, where stores reach memory out of program order. Which formal specification defines which reorderings a given architecture legally permits?
questions.explanation: A memory consistency model defines the legal orderings of loads and stores per architecture; x86's strong model allows fewer reorderings than ARM's weak one, which is why the bug only surfaced there.

questions.question: On a weakly ordered CPU, a producer writes data then a flag, yet the consumer sees flag = 1 with stale data. What must the producer insert between the two stores?
questions.explanation: A memory barrier (fence) orders the stores so the data is globally visible before the flag is, forbidding the CPU and compiler from reordering past it.

questions.question: Semaphore S starts at 1; three processes each call wait(S) once with no signal. What are S's final value and the number of blocked processes?
questions.explanation: Each wait decrements S: 1 -> 0 -> -1 -> -2. The first process enters; the other two block when S goes negative.

questions.question: Semaphore S starts at 2; the sequence wait, wait, wait, signal executes. What is S's final value?
questions.explanation: Three waits take S from 2 to -1, blocking the third process. The signal wakes it and restores S to 0, so all three proceed.

questions.question: In Lamport's Bakery algorithm, threads 3 and 5 both draw ticket number 7. Which thread enters its critical section first?
questions.explanation: Bakery orders contenders lexicographically on (ticket, ID); equal tickets fall to the smaller thread ID, so thread 3 precedes thread 5.

questions.question: Under the priority ceiling protocol, a priority-8 task holds resource A (ceiling 10). A priority-9 task then requests free resource B (ceiling 9). Is the request granted or blocked?
questions.explanation: PCP lets a task lock a new resource only if its priority exceeds the ceilings of all resources locked by others. A's ceiling is 10, above the requester's 9, so it blocks despite B being free.

questions.question: How many signal() calls are needed for four processes blocked on a counting semaphore to all proceed?
questions.explanation: Each signal wakes exactly one blocked process. Four blocked processes therefore require four signals to all continue.

questions.question: Two threads each execute counter++ 100,000 times on a shared counter initialized to 0, without synchronization. What is the smallest possible final value?
questions.explanation: Each increment is a non-atomic read-modify-write; interleavings can overwrite all but one increment per thread, leaving a minimum of 2.

questions.question: A producer's code was accidentally written as wait(mutex); wait(empty); ... With the buffer full and a consumer waiting for the mutex, what results?
questions.explanation: The producer holds mutex while blocked on empty; the consumer needs mutex to free a slot, so neither can proceed.

questions.question: In Peterson's solution, process 0 has set flag[0]=true and turn=1 while process 1 has not yet executed its entry code. Can process 0 enter its critical section?
questions.explanation: Process 0 waits while (flag[1] && turn==1); flag[1] is still false, so it skips the loop and enters.

questions.question: Why do Mesa-style condition variables require while(!condition) wait() instead of a single if?
questions.answer: The condition may be false when the waiter resumes
alternatives: Signal does not guarantee the condition still holds
questions.explanation: Mesa signals only wake a waiter; another thread can run first and falsify the condition, so it must be re-tested in a loop.

questions.question: A bounded buffer has capacity 10 with semaphores empty=10, full=0, and mutex=1. A producer deposits 4 items, then a consumer removes 1. What are the values of full and empty?
questions.explanation: Four deposits raise full to 4 and drop empty to 6; one removal drops full to 3 and raises empty to 7.
